title: Contravariance with in: consumers
goal: By the end you can recognise a consumer, declare it `in` in Kotlin (or write `? super` in Java), explain why a `Bin<Fruit>` can stand in for a `Bin<Apple>`, and choose `out` or `in` for any parameter with the PECS question.
opening:
Behind the fruit shop stands a compost bin. Bruised fruit goes in, any kind at all: apples, lemons, whatever is past selling. Nothing ever comes back out, and nobody has ever asked it to.

One morning a helper who is sorting apples asks for "a bin for bruised apples". You point at the compost bin. It's a perfectly good apple bin, because it takes every fruit, and so every apple.

Look at which way that went. The bin for any fruit stood in for the bin for apples. In the last lesson, the arrow ran the other way: an apple dispenser stood in for a fruit dispenser. It's natural to expect one direction for every generic type, and that's the trap. A type you only put things into turns the arrow around.

Covariance with out: producers ended with this bin. In this lesson, we'll write it in code with `in` and sort apples with one comparator for all fruit. Then we'll find the same flip inside function types, and finish with PECS, the rule Java programmers use to choose. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: `interface Bin<in T> { fun drop(item: T) }`. `compost` is a `Bin<Fruit>` that takes any fruit. A function needs a `Bin<Apple>`. Can you pass `compost`?
options: No: `Fruit` is the wider type, so a bin of `Fruit` can never stand in for a bin of `Apple`
Yes: a bin that takes every fruit also takes every apple
warmup.why: For a type that only takes values in, the arrow flips. The function will only ever drop apples in, and a bin for any fruit accepts all of them. `in` tells the compiler that `T` only goes in. `out` would be wrong, because a bin hands nothing out. Lesson 4's dispenser was the opposite case.

sections.h: A bin only takes fruit in, so the subtype arrow flips
sections.body:
A **consumer** is a type whose values of `T` only ever go in. (`T` is the type parameter, the blank on the label that each user of the type fills in.) The compost bin is a consumer. So is a `Comparator`, which takes two values and says which comes first. You hand a consumer a `T`, and it hands nothing typed `T` back.

Here is the bin in code. `drop` puts an item in. The shop's fruit are the same as in the last lesson: a `Fruit` interface with a `name` and a weight in `grams`, and `Apple` and `Lemon` as data classes that implement it. `throwOut` is the helper's job. It needs a bin for apples, and drops each bruised apple into it:

```java
interface Bin<T> {
    void drop(T item);
}

static void throwOut(List<Apple> apples, Bin<? super Apple> into) { ... }

Bin<Fruit> compost = f -> System.out.println("compost: " + f + ", " + f.getGrams() + " g");
throwOut(bruised, compost);              // fine: the parameter says ? super
Bin<Apple> strict = compost;             // error: Bin<Fruit> cannot be converted to Bin<Apple>
```

```kotlin
interface Bin<in T> {
    fun drop(item: T)
}

fun throwOut(apples: List<Apple>, into: Bin<Apple>) { ... }

val compost: Bin<Fruit> = CompostBin()
throwOut(bruised, compost)               // fine: Bin is declared in
val appleBin: Bin<Apple> = compost       // also fine
```

Run the substitution test from lesson 3 of this track, the question the compiler asks on every assignment: if I secretly hand over one type where another is expected, can any allowed call go wrong? A type that passes is a **subtype** of the other. `throwOut` expects a bin for apples, and you hand it the compost bin. Every call `throwOut` can make drops an `Apple`, and the compost bin takes every `Fruit`, so nothing can go wrong. `BinDemo` in the labs prints `compost: Gala, 180 g` and `compost: Fuji, 150 g`.

So for a consumer, the more general type is the one that stands in. The subtype arrow flips: `Apple` is a subtype of `Fruit`, but `Bin<Fruit>` is a subtype of `Bin<Apple>`. This is **contravariance**, the mirror image of lesson 4's covariance, where the arrow kept its direction. Kotlin declares it on the type parameter with **`in`**. Java has no such keyword, so it writes it at each use with a **wildcard**, a `?` that stands for a type it doesn't name. `? super Apple` reads "`Apple`, or a type above it, such as `Fruit` or `Object`". The figure puts the two cases side by side.

The other direction fails, and it should. A `Bin<Apple>` might be the pot for apple sauce, where the cook treats every item as an apple. Through a `Bin<Fruit>` view, someone could drop a lemon into the sauce. A lemon in the apple sauce is a mistake a kitchen only makes once:

```text
val back: Bin<Fruit> = appleBin
error: initializer type mismatch: expected 'Bin<Fruit>', actual 'Bin<Apple>'.
```

The rules for where `T` may appear are the mirror image of `out`, too. In a type declared `in T`, `T` may appear in parameters, which are in-positions, and not in return types or `val`s, which are out-positions. Add `fun last(): T` to `Bin`, and the compiler says `type parameter 'T' is declared as 'in' but occurs in 'out' position`. The reason mirrors lesson 4. Through a `Bin<Apple>` view of the compost bin, `last()` would promise an `Apple`, and the bin may be holding a lemon.

That's also where the bin picture breaks. A real compost bin gets tipped out every week, and anyone can see what's inside. A `Bin<in T>` gives you no typed way to look: through `in`, values only travel one way.

**A type that only takes `T` in can stand in wherever a narrower `T` is wanted. Say so with `in`.**

A bin you write yourself is the easy case. The consumer you'll meet most often was written by someone else, a long time ago.

sections.h: One comparator for all fruit: a Comparator takes values in
sections.body:
You already use the most common consumer: a **comparator**, an object whose `compare(a, b)` says which of two values comes first. It only *takes* values, two at a time, and hands back an `Int`. So a comparator written for all fruit works for apples, for lemons, for any subtype. Here is one that orders fruit by weight, used on a list of apples:

```java
Comparator<Fruit> byWeight = Comparator.comparingInt(Fruit::getGrams);

List<Apple> apples = new ArrayList<>(List.of(gala, fuji));
apples.sort(byWeight);                           // List<E>.sort(Comparator<? super E>)

Comparator<? super Apple> forApples = byWeight;  // fine
Comparator<Apple> strict = byWeight;             // error: Comparator<Fruit> cannot be converted to Comparator<Apple>
```

```kotlin
val byWeight: Comparator<Fruit> = compareBy { it.grams }

val apples = listOf(gala, fuji)
apples.sortedWith(byWeight)                      // sortedWith(comparator: Comparator<in T>)

val forApples: Comparator<in Apple> = byWeight   // fine
val strict: Comparator<Apple> = byWeight         // error: expected 'Comparator<Apple>', actual 'Comparator<Fruit>'
```

`ComparatorDemo` sorts two apples and two lemons with the one `byWeight`, and prints `[Fuji 150 g, Gala 180 g]` and `[Eureka 95 g, Eureka 120 g]`.

The last Kotlin line surprises people. If a comparator is a consumer, why isn't a `Comparator<Fruit>` simply a `Comparator<Apple>`, the way the compost bin was an apple bin? Because on the JVM, the machine that runs both Java and Kotlin code, Kotlin's `Comparator` *is* `java.util.Comparator`, a Java interface. Java has nowhere to write variance on a declaration, so Java interfaces have none. Kotlin treats `Comparator` as **invariant**, exactly as Java does: a `Comparator<Fruit>` and a `Comparator<Apple>` are simply unrelated types. It isn't Kotlin being stubborn. Nobody ever wrote the `in` down.

So the flexibility comes from the use site, the place where the type is used. The standard library declares `sortedWith(comparator: Comparator<in T>)`. That `in` inside the angle brackets of one parameter is Kotlin's spelling of Java's `? super T`, for that parameter only. Lesson 6 of this track calls it a type projection, and gives it a full lesson.

The JDK, Java's standard library, made the same choice everywhere. `List.sort`, `Collections.sort`, `Stream.sorted` and the `TreeMap` constructor all take a `Comparator<? super E>`. If you write your own ranking helper and forget the `? super` (or the `in`), it accepts only a comparator of the exact element type. The shop's shared `byWeight` no longer fits a list of apples, and the next person writes a second comparator that does the same thing.

Kotlin's own `Comparable` is different. It's the interface for types with a natural order, such as `Int` and `String`, and it's declared `interface Comparable<in T>`, with the `in` on the declaration. That is why lesson 2 of this track could call `maxOf2` on two `LocalDate`s: a `LocalDate` is a `Comparable<ChronoLocalDate>`, and so it also counts as a `Comparable<LocalDate>`.

**A parameter that only receives your values is a consumer. Give it `in`, or `? super` in Java.**

The lab's `highest(items: List<T>, comparator: Comparator<in T>)` is the shape to copy. A comparator takes two values and returns a number. A plain function takes values too, and the same flip hides inside its type.

sections.h: Function types: in on the left of the arrow, out on the right
sections.body:
A **function type** such as `(Fruit) -> String` is the type of a function value: a lambda you can store in a variable and call later. Behind the arrow notation, Kotlin writes it as `Function1<in P, out R>`. The function takes its parameter in, so it's a consumer of `P`. It hands its result out, so it's a producer of `R`. A function type is contravariant on the left of the arrow and covariant on the right.

Picture the shop's scale. A scale that weighs any fruit can stand in for a scale that only weighs apples. A function that writes a price card for any fruit can stand in for one that writes cards for apples. The `String` it returns is certainly an `Any`, too:

```java
// Java's Consumer and Function are plain invariant interfaces, so say it at the use site:
Consumer<Fruit> weighAny = f -> System.out.println("scale: " + f + ", " + f.getGrams() + " g");
Function<Fruit, String> label = f -> "price card for " + f;

Consumer<? super Apple> weighApple = weighAny;                   // fine
Function<? super Apple, ? extends Object> appleLabel = label;    // fine
Consumer<Apple> strict = weighAny;    // error: Consumer<Fruit> cannot be converted to Consumer<Apple>
```

```kotlin
val weighAny: (Fruit) -> Unit = { println("scale: $it, ${it.grams} g") }
val label: (Fruit) -> String = { "price card for $it" }

val weighApple: (Apple) -> Unit = weighAny     // fine: takes more general input
val appleLabel: (Apple) -> Any = label         // fine: in on the left, out on the right
val tooBroad: (Fruit) -> Unit = weighApple     // error: expected '(Fruit) -> Unit', actual '(Apple) -> Unit'
```

`HandlerDemo` prints `scale: Gala, 180 g` and `price card for Fuji`. The last line fails for the apple-sauce reason: a scale for apples only, used as a scale for any fruit, could be handed a lemon. The flip is also why the lab's `DeliveryBell<Apple>` accepts a listener written for every `Fruit`, with no extra work.

Function types explain the odd cases from lesson 4 of this track, too: the ones where a `T` inside a parameter was allowed in an `out` type. Follow the value. In `fun each(f: (T) -> Unit)`, the class calls `f` and hands it a `T`, so the `T` travels out of the class, even though it sits inside a parameter. In `fun handler(): (T) -> Unit`, the class hands a function to the caller, and the caller feeds it a `T`, so the `T` travels in.

To get the same answer without tracing, give each position a sign. An out-position is `+`, and an in-position is `−`. When one type sits inside another, multiply the signs. A plain parameter is `−`. The parameter of a function that is itself a parameter is `−` times `−`, which is `+`:

| Member in `class C<…T>` | Where `T` sits | Sign | Legal under `out T` | Legal under `in T` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `fun get(): T` | return | + | yes | no |
| `fun put(t: T)` | parameter | − | no | yes |
| `fun each(f: (T) -> Unit)` | parameter of a parameter | − × − = + | yes | no |
| `fun handler(): (T) -> Unit` | parameter of the result | + × − = − | no | yes |
| `fun putAll(xs: List<T>)` | `List<out E>` in a parameter | − × + = − | no | yes |

You won't need the table often. Use it when an error points at a lambda parameter and your intuition runs out. The `SortingBin` interface in the demo has three members to try it on.

The table is the full theory. Java programmers carry a shorter version of it around, in four letters.

sections.h: PECS: Java's four-letter name for out and in
sections.body:
Java programmers learn variance as **PECS**: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. It comes from Joshua Bloch's book *Effective Java* (Item 31), and the Kotlin docs cite it as the background for `out` and `in`. A producer parameter gives you values, so it gets `? extends`. A consumer parameter takes your values, so it gets `? super`. The mapping onto Kotlin is one to one:

| Role of the parameter | Java | Kotlin |
|---|---|---|
| gives you `T` values (producer) | `? extends T` | `out T` |
| takes `T` values from you (consumer) | `? super T` | `in T` |
| both | `T` | `T` |

Here is a copy helper with one of each. `from` is a list the helper only reads, a producer. `to` is a list the helper only adds to, a consumer. The test copies the morning's apples onto the shop shelf, which already holds a lemon, and into a list of anything, which already holds a paper bag:

```java
// java.util.Collections:
// public static <T> void copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)

static <T> void copyInto(List<? extends T> from, List<? super T> to) {
    for (T x : from) to.add(x);
}

copyInto(apples, shelf);                    // a List<Apple> into a List<Fruit>
copyInto(shelf, new ArrayList<Apple>());    // error: method copyInto ... cannot be applied to given types
```

```kotlin
fun <T> copyInto(from: List<T>, to: MutableList<in T>) {
    for (x in from) to.add(x)
}

copyInto(apples, shelf)                     // a List<Apple> into a MutableList<Fruit>
copyInto(shelf, mutableListOf<Apple>())     // error: actual type is 'MutableList<Apple>', but 'MutableList<in Fruit>' was expected
```

`PecsDemo` prints `shelf = [Eureka, Gala, Fuji], anything = [a paper bag, Gala, Fuji]`. The last line fails, and it's the crate of lesson 3 again. Copying a shelf of mixed fruit into a crate of apples would drop the lemon into the crate.

The Kotlin version needs only one `in`, on `to`. `from` is a read-only `List`, which is already declared `out`, so writing `List<out T>` would only earn a warning that the `out` is redundant. Java needs both wildcards, because none of its types carries its own variance.

When you design a signature, ask one question per parameter. Does this parameter *give* me values of `T`, *take* values of `T` from me, or both? Give: `out`, or `? extends`. Take: `in`, or `? super`. Both: plain `T`.

**Ask each parameter whether it gives you `T`, takes `T`, or both. The answer picks `out`, `in` or plain `T`.**

A wrong answer is rarely a compile error in your own code, and your own tests pass. It shows up later, as a caller who can't pass a perfectly good `Comparator<Fruit>`, and writes a cast to get around you.

The question has a limit, and `copyInto` has just met it. A `MutableList` both gives and takes, so it can't be declared `out` or `in`. The `MutableList<in T>` on `to` is a use-site projection: `MutableList` itself stays invariant, and this one parameter asks for a drop-only view of it. The next lesson is about those views.

compare.title: A consumer, declared once in Kotlin, spelled at each use in Java

java.title: Bins.java

kotlin.title: Bins.kt

compare.note: The rule is the same in both languages: through a contravariant view you may put values in, but you get nothing typed back out. Java puts `? super` on every consumer parameter. Kotlin puts `in` on the consumer's declaration once, and its function types are contravariant in their parameters from the start. The one trap is a Java interface used from Kotlin. `Comparator`, `Consumer` and every other Java interface have no declared variance, so Kotlin treats them as invariant, and you need a use-site `in` (`Comparator<in T>`) exactly where Java needs `? super T`. When Java calls Kotlin, a parameter of type `Bin<Fruit>` shows up as `Bin<? super Fruit>`.

worked.title: Build a delivery bell that accepts general listeners

steps.say: The shop has a bell by the back door. When a delivery arrives, the bell calls everyone who asked to be told, once for each item. The sign-writer listens for apples, to write a card for each variety. The stock-keeper counts every fruit, whatever it is. You want both of them on the bell for apple deliveries. Start by naming the roles: the bell hands each item out, and each listener takes it in.

1. Write `listen` with the listener as a consumer of `E`. In Kotlin, a function type already has `in` on its parameter, so `(E) -> Unit` is enough. In Java, a plain `Consumer<E>` would turn the stock-keeper away, so write `Consumer<? super E>`.

2. Wire it up. Both listeners join the bell for apples. Self-check before reading on: why can't the sign-writer listen to a `DeliveryBell<Fruit>`? (That bell may ring with a lemon, and `appleSign` was written for apples only.)
steps.code:
val apples = DeliveryBell<Apple>()
apples.listen(appleSign)
apples.listen(stockCount)               // fine: a (Fruit) -> Unit is an (Apple) -> Unit
apples.ring(Apple("Gala", 180))         // 2

val allFruit = DeliveryBell<Fruit>()
allFruit.listen(appleSign)
// error: argument type mismatch: actual type is '(Apple) -> Unit',
//        but '(Fruit) -> Unit' was expected.

lab.title: Consumers: a contravariant Bin, a comparator for all fruit, a delivery bell
steps: Read `Fruit.kt`: the same `Fruit`, `Apple` and `Lemon` as in this lesson. Then run the tests. All eight fail. The variance test says `expected: "Bin<? super Fruit>"` but `was: "Bin<Fruit>"`: the test reads the Java signature of `dropAll`, and Java sees no wildcard while `Bin` is invariant.

In `Bin.kt`, add `in` to `Bin`'s type parameter. Then write `CollectingBin`: keep a private `ArrayList<T>`, and return a copy from `items`. Why can't `CollectingBin` itself be declared `in T`? (Hint: look at `items`.)
In `Sorting.kt`, write `highest` with a loop and `comparator.compare`. The test calls it with a `List<Apple>` and `byWeight`, a `Comparator<Fruit>`.

`DeliveryBell.kt` is the bell by the back door: listeners sign up with `listen`, and `ring` hands one delivered item to each of them. Store the listeners in a private list, and call them in order in `ring`.
Run the tests until all eight pass.
hints: `CollectingBin<T>` hands `T` back out through `items`, so its own `T` is both in and out. The class stays invariant; only the `Bin` interface it implements is `in`.
`dropped.toList()` returns a copy, which is what the snapshot test checks.
`private val listeners = ArrayList<(E) -> Unit>()` is all the storage `DeliveryBell` needs.

drill.title: Pick out or in for five parameters
drill.prompt: Close this page. For each parameter, write the Kotlin type and the Java type with the right variance: (1) `source`, a list you only read fruit from; (2) `bag`, a mutable list you only add fruit to; (3) `order`, a comparator of fruit; (4) `onArrival`, a function called with each fruit that arrives; (5) `crate`, a mutable list you both read from and add to.

answer.src:
fun stockUp(
    source: List<Fruit>,                  // 1: List is already out
    bag: MutableList<in Fruit>,           // 2: a drop-only view
    order: Comparator<in Fruit>,          // 3: java.util.Comparator needs a use-site in
    onArrival: (Fruit) -> Unit,           // 4: function parameters are already in
    crate: MutableList<Fruit>             // 5: read and write: invariant
) { }

alt.title: StockUp.java
alt.src:
static void stockUp(
        List<? extends Fruit> source,           // 1: producer extends
        List<? super Fruit> bag,                // 2: consumer super
        Comparator<? super Fruit> order,        // 3: consumer super
        Consumer<? super Fruit> onArrival,      // 4: consumer super
        List<Fruit> crate) {                    // 5: both: no wildcard
}

recap: A consumer only takes values of `T` in. A consumer of a supertype can stand in for a consumer of a subtype, the way the compost bin is an apple bin: the arrow flips. That is contravariance.
Kotlin declares it once, with `in T` on the declaration, and Java writes `? super T` at each use. In an `in` type, `T` may appear in parameters, not in return types or `val`s.
Function types are `Function1<in P, out R>`, so a `(Fruit) -> Unit` is an `(Apple) -> Unit`. When a `T` hides inside a lambda parameter, multiply the signs: − × − = +.
`java.util.Comparator` is a Java interface, so Kotlin treats it as invariant. Write `Comparator<in T>` in your signatures, as `sortedWith` does.
PECS: Producer Extends (`out`), Consumer Super (`in`). Ask of each parameter: does it give me `T`, take `T`, or both?
The limit: `in` only fits a type whose `T` never comes out. A type that gives and takes, such as `MutableList`, can declare neither, and needs a projection where it's used.
closing:
We started at the compost bin, which takes any fruit and so makes a fine apple bin. `in T` writes that down: `T` only goes in, so a `Bin<Fruit>` can stand in for a `Bin<Apple>`, and the arrow flips. Comparators and function parameters are consumers too, and PECS is the same idea in Java's spelling.

Now look in your own code for a parameter typed `Comparator<X>` or `Consumer<X>`, with no `in` or `? super`. Each one turns away a perfectly good general handler.

Next, we'll take a crate that both gives and takes, and tell one helper, for one job, to treat it as take-only. How do you get variance out of a type that can't declare any?

quiz.q: `interface Bin<in T> { fun drop(item: T) }`. Which assignment compiles?
quiz.why: With `in`, the arrow flips: a bin for the supertype is a bin for the subtype. The reverse is unsafe. An apple-only bin seen as a `Bin<Fruit>` could be handed a lemon, the lemon in the apple sauce.

quiz.q: Which member can you add to `interface Bin<in T>`?
quiz.why: `dropAll` takes the items in: `List<out E>` inside a parameter is − × + = −, an in-position. `last()` and `inside` hand a `T` out. In `forEachInside`, the `T` is the parameter of a parameter (− × − = +), so it is an out-position too.

quiz.q: Kotlin: `val byWeight: Comparator<Fruit> = compareBy { it.grams }`. Why does `val c: Comparator<Apple> = byWeight` fail?
options: Comparators are covariant, so the arrow goes the other way
`Comparator` is `java.util.Comparator`, a Java interface with no declared variance, so Kotlin treats it as invariant
quiz.why: Kotlin can't add variance to a Java interface, so `Comparator<Fruit>` and `Comparator<Apple>` are unrelated until you project: `Comparator<in Apple>`. The standard library does that in `sortedWith(comparator: Comparator<in T>)`. Kotlin's own `Comparable` is declared `in T`, and behaves the other way.

quiz.q: Java: you write `static void onDelivery(Consumer<Apple> listener)`. A teammate has a `Consumer<Fruit>` that counts the stock. What is the right fix?
options: Change the parameter to `Consumer<? super Apple>`
Change the parameter to `Consumer<? extends Apple>`
Ask the teammate to cast their listener
Change the parameter to a raw `Consumer`
quiz.why: The listener consumes the apples you pass it, so Consumer Super. `? extends Apple` would accept a consumer of some unknown subtype of `Apple`, which you could never safely hand a plain apple. A raw type turns the checks off altogether.

quiz.q: From "Covariance with out: producers": why is `fun <R> map(f: (T) -> R): Tray<R>` allowed inside `class Tray<out T>`?
options: Because `map` has its own type parameter, which exempts the whole method
Because `T` is the parameter of `f`, which is itself a parameter: two in-positions make an out-position
Because the variance check skips functions that return a new object
quiz.why: The tray calls `f` and passes it a `T`, so values of `T` flow out of the tray. By the sign rule, − × − = +. A new type parameter `R` doesn't exempt anything: `fun <R> bad(t: T): R` would still fail.

flashcards.front: What makes a generic type safe to declare `in T`?
flashcards.back: It only takes values of `T` in, through parameters. No public member returns a `T`.

flashcards.front: With `Bin<in T>`, which way does the arrow go between `Bin<Fruit>` and `Bin<Apple>`?
flashcards.back: `Bin<Fruit>` is a subtype of `Bin<Apple>`: the arrow flips.

flashcards.front: Kotlin's `in T` corresponds to what in Java?
flashcards.back: `? super T`, written at the use site, such as `Consumer<? super Apple>`.

flashcards.front: Is `(Fruit) -> Unit` a subtype of `(Apple) -> Unit`?
flashcards.back: Yes. Function types are `Function1<in P, out R>`, so a function for the general type fits where one for the specific type is expected.

flashcards.front: Why must Kotlin code write `Comparator<in T>` instead of plain `Comparator<T>`?
flashcards.back: On the JVM, `Comparator` is the Java interface `java.util.Comparator`, which has no declared variance, so Kotlin treats it as invariant.
Producer Extends, Consumer Super (Effective Java, Item 31). In Kotlin: producer `out`, consumer `in`.

flashcards.front: Sign rule: where does `T` sit in `fun each(f: (T) -> Unit)`?
flashcards.back: Parameter of a parameter: − × − = +, an out-position. Legal under `out T`, illegal under `in T`.

terms.plain: A type whose `T` values only go in: bins, comparators, listeners.
`C<Super>` is a subtype of `C<Sub>`: the arrow flips.
Kotlin's keyword on a type parameter: "T only goes into this type".
Java's use-site wildcard for a consumer: "T or any supertype of T".
Producer Extends, Consumer Super: the Java rule for choosing wildcards.
The type behind `(P) -> R`: contravariant in the parameter, covariant in the result.
Out-positions are +, in-positions are −; multiply through nesting to find where `T` really sits.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate asks: "Why is a bin of Fruit a subtype of a bin of Apple? That's backwards." Explain it in your own words, and say how you'd write the same idea in Java.
explain_back.answer: Subtyping means "can be used wherever the other is expected without anything going wrong". Code that expects a bin for apples will only ever drop apples into it. A bin that accepts every fruit accepts those too, so it can stand in safely. The opposite swap is unsafe: an apple-only bin, used as a bin for all fruit, could be handed a lemon. So for things that only take values in, the general one stands in for the specific one, and the arrow points the other way from the element types. Kotlin declares this once, with `interface Bin<in T>`. Java writes it at each use as `Bin<? super Apple>`, which is the Consumer Super half of PECS.

deeper.body:
Contravariance explains a detail of Kotlin's `Comparable`. It is declared `public interface Comparable<in T>`. So when Kotlin writes a Java signature for `fun <T : Comparable<T>> max(a: T, b: T)`, the bound becomes `<T extends Comparable<? super T>>`, the same bound the JDK writes by hand in `Collections.max`. That is how `LocalDate`, a `Comparable<ChronoLocalDate>`, gets through a bound that says `Comparable<LocalDate>`.

The sign rule also covers type arguments of variant classes. Inside `class C<out T>`, a parameter of type `Comparable<T>` is allowed: the parameter is −, and `Comparable`'s `in` is −, so `T` ends up in a + position. A parameter of type `MutableList<T>` is not allowed in either kind of class. An invariant argument counts as 0, and anything times 0 stays 0, which is neither in nor out.

C# uses the same keywords, `in` and `out`, for interfaces and delegates, which is where Kotlin borrowed them. Scala writes `+T` and `-T`, the signs from the table.

One caution for Java callers. When Java calls a Kotlin function with a parameter `listener: (Fruit) -> Unit`, it sees `Function1<? super Fruit, Unit>`. A Java lambda fits that type, but it must return `Unit.INSTANCE`. Kotlin APIs meant for Java callers often take a Java functional interface instead, or declare a `fun interface` of their own.
